strengths: Provides a clean theoretical connection between the proposed star-shaped sampler and ReMDM (showing equivalence at σt = 1−αs), which explains why the method avoids the costly per-schedule hyperparameter search that ReMDM requires — a genuine practical advantage that is empirically substantiated in Appendix C.1.

The paper decomposes and validates each design choice through careful, well-designed ablations: optimal activation time for the star-shaped phase (Fig. 2), loop-size vs. quality/diversity trade-offs (Fig. 5), error-predictor temperature (Fig. 6), and error-predictor capacity (Table 1), giving good insight into why the method works and how to configure it.

Demonstrates practical value at scale: integrating G-Star into a 7B instruction-tuned model (Dream-Instruct) with only a lightweight, frozen-backbone classification head yields consistent, non-trivial gains across seven diverse downstream benchmarks (MMLU, GPQA, IFEval, etc.), suggesting the method generalizes beyond small-scale unconditional text generation.

Method is compatible with pretrained MDLM checkpoints without requiring full retraining (only a lightweight error predictor), and the training/inference procedures (Algorithms 1–2) are clearly specified, aiding reproducibility; code and detailed hyperparameters are provided in the appendix.

Qualitative analyses (Figs. 7–9) convincingly show that the guided sampler produces structured, phrase-level coherent edits rather than the scattered, unstructured remasking of the unguided baseline, supporting the core mechanistic claim of the paper.

The few-step/medium-step regime results (Fig. 3, Table 1, Table 2) show substantial and consistent improvements over both MDLM and tuned ReMDM baselines, addressing a practically important setting (fast sampling) for discrete diffusion models.
weaknesses: The core theoretical device (star-shaped diffusion) is adapted directly from prior work (Okhotin et al., 2023) and largely reduces to a known equivalence with an existing method (ReMDM with a specific σt schedule); the incremental technical novelty beyond the error-predictor add-on is limited.

MAUVE, the primary headline metric, is shown by the authors' own analysis (Appendix C.2/C.3) to be non-monotonic and to trade off against diversity in complicated, task-dependent ways; several reported "best" configurations (e.g., 512 vs 256 steps in Table 1) appear to be selecting favorable points on this trade-off curve rather than reflecting a robust, single notion of quality, which could overstate practical gains.

Despite criticizing ReMDM for requiring extensive per-schedule tuning of η, the proposed method itself relies on several manually tuned, task/dataset-specific hyperparameters (ton, αon, τremask, loop size, refinement fraction — see Table 4 and Appendix D), and it is unclear how sensitive final results are to these choices or how they would be selected for a genuinely new task without a validation set matching the eval metric.

The large-scale evaluation baseline (Dream-Instruct 7B) shows non-trivial discrepancies from the originally published numbers (e.g., IFEval 62.5 vs. reproduced 56.4), which is disclosed but not fully explained, weakening confidence in the fairness/comparability of the +G-Star improvements on that benchmark.

Code-generation evaluation relies solely on conditional perplexity under an external LM (Qwen2.5-Coder) rather than functional correctness metrics (e.g., pass@k), which is a weaker proxy for code quality and limits the strength of the code-generation claims.

The formal proof of Claim 1 is a relatively straightforward derivation (essentially algebraic simplification of a KL term between two categorical interpolations) and is presented with some informal/loose steps; its contribution to the paper's significance is modest.

No explicit wall-clock/compute overhead comparison is given for the additional error-predictor forward pass during sampling, even though parameter overhead is mentioned qualitatively; a quantitative latency comparison would strengthen the efficiency claims.

strengths: Provides a clean theoretical grounding: proves the star-shaped sampler's VLB reduces to the same functional form as the standard masked diffusion objective (Claim 1/Appendix A.1), and shows a formal equivalence to ReMDM under a specific remasking schedule (Proposition 1/Appendix A.2), which explains why the sampler can reuse off-the-shelf pretrained MDLM checkpoints without full retraining.

Extensive and thoughtful ablation studies: identification of the optimal activation point for remasking (Fig. 1-2), guided vs. unguided comparison across sampling-step budgets (Fig. 3-4), loop-size ablation, temperature trade-off analysis, error-predictor capacity/efficiency study, and cross-domain robustness evaluation of the predictor (Table 3) — this level of analysis is unusually thorough for a sampler-focused paper.

Broad empirical validation spanning unconditional text generation (OpenWebText), conditional code generation (Conala), and a large-scale 7B instruction-tuned model (Dream-Instruct) across seven diverse downstream benchmarks, demonstrating general applicability beyond toy settings.

Practical efficiency considerations are well documented: a head-only (frozen backbone) predictor variant achieves near-parity with full fine-tuning while incurring negligible parameter overhead, and Appendix D provides a careful wall-clock/NFE accounting showing the method's cost scales as a controlled (1+ΔB/D) factor over the base sampler.

Good qualitative analysis (Figs. 9-13) contrasting scattered/unstructured unguided remasking against the more structured, phrase-level corrections made by the guided sampler, which supports the core mechanistic claim.

Transparent limitations section (in-place substitution only, no insert/delete, separate sequential predictor training, no integration with orthogonal inference-acceleration techniques) and a reproducibility statement with code and detailed hyperparameter appendices.
weaknesses: The core theoretical novelty is tempered by Proposition 1, which shows the base star-shaped sampler is mathematically equivalent to ReMDM under a specific schedule; the primary distinguishing contribution is therefore the learned error predictor, which narrows the paper's novelty relative to its framing.

Differentiation from concurrent, closely related work (Kim et al. 2025; Huang et al. 2025) is limited to a short qualitative paragraph with no empirical comparison, making it hard to assess the relative benefit of the proposed design choices (star-shaped decoupling + targeted error detection) versus these alternatives.

Evaluation relies heavily on automatic proxy metrics (generative perplexity via GPT-2, MAUVE, Diversity, conditional perplexity via Qwen-Coder) without any human evaluation; these metrics are known to be imperfect measures of text/code quality, especially for judging subtle coherence gains claimed by the qualitative examples.

Gains on the large-scale Dream-Instruct 7B benchmarks (Table 1) are numerically modest (mostly ~1-2 points) and reported as single-run point estimates without variance/error bars or statistical significance testing, making it hard to judge whether improvements are reliable versus noise.

The method still introduces multiple hyperparameters requiring tuning per task/schedule (activation time t_on, denoiser temperature, error-predictor temperature, loop size), and while the paper argues this is less burdensome than ReMDM's η, no direct quantitative comparison of tuning cost/robustness across settings is provided.

The error predictor is trained to detect errors of a specific pretrained diffusion model via simulated denoising; while cross-domain robustness within the same base model is tested (Table 3), transferability of a predictor across different diffusion backbones/architectures is not evaluated.

Code-generation benchmarking (Table 2) omits several baselines used in the OWT comparison (e.g., DDPD, confidence-based planners), making the code-domain evidence less comprehensive than the language-domain evidence.
